title: Given a set of distinct numbers, generate all possible subsets, including the empty set and the full set. Explain the iterative doubling technique that builds subsets one element at a time.
shortTitle: Subsets (Generate All Subsets of a Distinct Set)

s1_definition.profdef: Subsets is the foundational Subsets-pattern problem. For a set of n distinct elements there are exactly two to the power n subsets. The iterative technique starts with a list containing only the empty subset and, for each new element, duplicates every existing subset and adds the element to each duplicate. This doubles the collection with each element, naturally producing all subsets in O(2^n) total work, which is optimal because that many subsets must be output.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a customer like Rajesh can opt into any combination of add-on services, say overdraft, insurance, and a rewards card. We want every possible service bundle he could choose, from choosing nothing to choosing all three. We start with one empty bundle, and for each new service we copy every bundle we have so far and add the service to each copy, so the number of bundles doubles each time.
s1_definition.oneliner: Start with the empty subset and, for each element, duplicate all existing subsets and add the element to each copy.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Subsets is the foundational Subsets-pattern problem. For a set of n distinct elements there are exactly two to the power n subsets. The iterative technique starts with a list containing only the empty subset and, for each new element, duplicates every existing subset and adds the element to each duplicate. This doubles the collection with each element, naturally producing all subsets in O(2^n) total work, which is optimal because that many subsets must be output.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a customer like Rajesh can opt into any combination of add-on services, say overdraft, insurance, and a rewards card. We want every possible service bundle he could choose, from choosing nothing to choosing all three. We start with one empty bundle, and for each new service we copy every bundle we have so far and add the service to each copy, so the number of bundles doubles each time.

**One line to remember:** Start with the empty subset and, for each element, duplicate all existing subsets and add the element to each copy.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep a list of subsets, seeded with one empty list. For each incoming number we record the current size, then iterate over exactly that many existing subsets, copying each and appending the new number. For example, `int size = subsets.size(); for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) { List<Integer> copy = new ArrayList<>(subsets.get(i)); copy.add(num); subsets.add(copy); }`. Capturing the size first is essential so we iterate only over the pre-existing subsets and not the ones we are adding in this round.

This produces all subsets without recursion, which avoids stack depth concerns for larger inputs. Each subset is a fresh list, so later rounds that extend subsets never mutate earlier results.

A senior-level nuance is that the elements are assumed distinct; duplicates require a different approach that skips over-counting. Another nuance is that the output size is inherently exponential, so the algorithm is optimal in the sense that it spends time proportional to the size of what it must produce, and one should warn that enumerating subsets of a large set is infeasible by nature, not by implementation.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India offers Rajesh a set of distinct add-on services, and the product team wants to enumerate every possible bundle he could select, including the empty bundle, to price and present options. This is exactly how Subsets works: each bundle is a subset of the available services.

Problem 2 — Building bundles by hand is error-prone and misses combinations. This is why we generate them systematically by doubling: each new service copies every existing bundle and adds itself, guaranteeing completeness.

The code defines a `SubsetsService` exposing `allBundles(services)` returning a list of service-name lists. A `Demo` enumerates every bundle for three National Bank of India add-on services and logs them.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: services Overdraft, Insurance, Rewards.

Step 1: Start with one bundle, the empty bundle, so the list is [[]].

Step 2: Add Overdraft. Copy the one existing bundle and add Overdraft, giving [[], [Overdraft]]. The list doubled to two.

Step 3: Add Insurance. Copy both existing bundles and add Insurance, giving [[], [Overdraft], [Insurance], [Overdraft, Insurance]]. The list doubled to four.

Step 4: Add Rewards. Copy all four existing bundles and add Rewards, giving eight bundles total, including the empty bundle and the full bundle Overdraft, Insurance, Rewards.

Step 5: The final list holds all eight bundles, which is two to the power three.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Subsets is the foundational problem of the Subsets pattern: given a set of distinct elements I generate all two-to-the-n subsets, including the empty set and the full set. I use the iterative doubling technique. I start with a collection containing only the empty subset, and for each new element I take a snapshot of the current collection size, then copy every existing subset and add the new element to each copy. Each element therefore doubles the collection, and after processing all elements I have exactly every subset.

The one detail that trips people up is capturing the size before the round begins. If I iterated over the live collection while adding to it, I would process subsets I just created and over-generate, so I snapshot the size first and extend only the pre-existing subsets. I also make each subset a fresh copy so extending subsets in a later round never mutates an earlier result.

At the National Bank of India I used this to enumerate every add-on service bundle a customer like Rajesh could choose, from the empty bundle to the full bundle, so the product team could price and present all options. I generated the bundles by doubling as each service was considered, which guaranteed completeness without recursion. Explaining the snapshot-the-size subtlety and acknowledging that the output is inherently exponential, so the method is optimal for what it must produce, is what shows an interviewer I understand both the technique and its limits.
